cards.front: What must every virus particle contain, and what protects its genetic material?
cards.back: Every virus has a **genome** of DNA or RNA, enclosed by a protective protein **capsid**. Capsid proteins also help give the virus its shape.
cards.hint: Two components: one genetic, one protein.

cards.front: Why does a virus infect some cells but not others?
cards.back: Its viral **attachment protein** must bind a matching **receptor** on the host cell surface. This match helps set the virus's host range.

cards.front: Why can a virus not reproduce without a host cell?
cards.back: It lacks its own **ribosomes** and metabolism, so it uses host ribosomes, energy and materials to make new genomes and proteins.
cards.hint: What machinery does a virus lack?

cards.front: What is an envelope in a virus?
cards.back: An **envelope** is a lipid membrane surrounding the capsid of some viruses. It derives from a host-cell membrane during budding or intracellular assembly.
cards.hint: Some viruses have it, others do not.

cards.back: An **attachment protein** is a viral surface protein that binds to a host cell. It binds to a receptor on the host cell.
cards.hint: It is found on the virus surface.

cards.front: Outline the routes by which a viral genome can enter a host cell after attachment.
cards.back: Enveloped viruses may fuse their envelope with the cell membrane. Other viruses are taken up into a **membrane-bound compartment**. Some inject their genome while the capsid stays outside.
cards.hint: Three different routes, depending on the virus.

cards.front: Outline how a virus makes new particles inside a host cell.
cards.back: The viral genome directs production of viral nucleic acid and proteins, using host ribosomes and resources. New genomes and proteins **assemble** into particles, which leave by cell rupture or release from the membrane.

cards.front: Why does a viral infection not always kill the host cell straight away?
cards.back: Some viral genomes **persist** inside the cell before producing new particles. In some cases viral DNA becomes part of the host genome, which delays cell destruction.

cards.front: Is it enough for a virus to bind a receptor on a cell to infect it?
cards.back: No. A **receptor** match does not guarantee infection. The cell must also support the later stages, so the virus can use the cell to produce its components.
cards.hint: Attachment is only the first step.

cards.back: **Ribosomes** are cellular structures that make proteins by translating genetic instructions.
cards.hint: Found in cells, used by viruses.

cards.front: How do viruses and living cells compare in how they reproduce?
cards.back: Cells divide using their own machinery and cytoplasm. Viruses use host machinery to make components that **assemble** into new particles. Both have inheritable genetic material.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say a virus is alive just because it has genetic material that can vary and be inherited?
cards.back: Cells also have inheritable genetic material, but a virus lacks independent **metabolism** and cannot grow or reproduce outside a host. Viruses are therefore usually described as non-living.
cards.hint: Consider what a virus cannot do alone.

cards.back: **Metabolism** is the collection of chemical reactions that sustain a cell. Viruses lack their own metabolism.
